posts.title: Why We're Leaving America
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A map showing the US and potential destination countries with pins marking Costa Rica, Portugal, and Thailand
posts.excerpt: After years of watching our savings buy less and less, we made the decision that changes everything. Here's why we're leaving the country we've called home our entire lives.
posts.content:
It didn't happen overnight. For years we watched our grocery bills climb, our property taxes rise, and our retirement accounts struggle to keep pace with inflation. We sat down one evening with a spreadsheet — something we'd done a hundred times before — but this time the numbers told a different story. What if we didn't stay? What if retirement didn't have to mean scraping by in a country where the cost of living keeps climbing faster than our fixed income ever could?

That question opened a door we hadn't let ourselves look through before. We started researching countries where our retirement savings would go further, where healthcare is affordable, where a couple could live well on what we've worked forty years to build. The more we learned, the more the answer became obvious. This isn't about running away from America. It's about running toward a retirement we can actually enjoy — with financial security, peace of mind, and the adventure we've been putting off for too long.

We know this decision will surprise some people. Our kids needed time to process it. Our friends think we're either brave or crazy — maybe both. But once you see a path to a better retirement, one where you're not constantly anxious about money, it's hard to unsee it. This blog is our way of documenting the journey, sharing what we learn, and hopefully helping others who are asking themselves the same question: what if there's a better way?

posts.title: Our Retirement Timeline — The Countdown Begins
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A calendar with dates circled and a plane icon marking December 2027
posts.excerpt: Denise has a date locked in. Brent is five years behind. Here's our plan for making two retirements work on one timeline.
posts.content:
Denise retires in December 2027. That's not a hope or a goal — it's the date she handed in to HR. After thirty-two years in public education, she's ready to trade lesson plans for travel plans. Her pension vests fully at the end of the 2027 calendar year, and she's giving the maximum notice out of respect for her school, but make no mistake: that last day is circled in red on our calendar.

My timeline is different. I turn sixty in 2031, and my Social Security benefit nearly doubles if I wait until full retirement age. The plan is for Denise to move abroad first — we'll decide exactly where in the coming months — and I'll join her permanently once I wrap up my consulting work. We'll do the long-distance thing for a while, visiting every six to eight weeks. It's not ideal, but running the numbers, this staggered approach gives us an extra twenty-three hundred dollars a month in combined benefits. That's real money when you're living on a fixed income.

Between now and Denise's departure, we're in full preparation mode. Downsizing the house, selling the second car, sorting through thirty years of accumulated stuff. We're aiming to reduce our monthly overhead by at least forty percent before she steps on that plane. Every dollar we cut now is a dollar we don't have to worry about later. The countdown is on, and honestly, it feels more exciting than scary.

posts.title: Top 5 Countries We're Considering for Retirement
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A world map with five highlighted regions: Western Europe, Central America, Southeast Asia, and Southern Europe
posts.excerpt: We've narrowed the list to five countries that check our boxes: affordable healthcare, reasonable cost of living, safety, and a welcoming visa path for retirees.
posts.content:
Portugal has been at the top of our list since the beginning. The D7 passive income visa is straightforward for retirees with a modest pension, the healthcare system ranks among the best in Europe, and you can live comfortably in the Algarve or the Silver Coast for around two thousand dollars a month. The climate is mild year-round, and the English proficiency is high enough that we wouldn't struggle while learning Portuguese.

Costa Rica offers something different — proximity to the US, a well-established expat community, and a universal healthcare system that permanent residents can access after a waiting period. The pensionado visa requires proof of just one thousand dollars per month in lifetime income. We'd be close enough to fly back for family events, and the biodiversity is incredible if you love nature. The main downside is the higher cost of living compared to other options on our list.

Panama runs on the dollar, which eliminates currency risk entirely, and its Pensionado visa is famously generous — permanent residency with discounts on everything from medical bills to utility costs. The city of Boquete has a thriving retiree community and a spring-like climate year-round. Malaysia's MM2H program and Thailand's retirement visa round out our top five. Both offer extremely low costs of living — we're talking twelve to fifteen hundred dollars a month for a very comfortable lifestyle — along with excellent private healthcare at a fraction of US prices.

We're planning a scouting trip in early 2027 to visit at least three of these countries. Each one has trade-offs, and we want to experience them firsthand before making a decision that will shape the rest of our lives.

posts.title: How Much Does It Really Cost to Live Abroad?
posts.author: Brent & Denise
posts.alt: A comparison chart showing monthly expenses in US dollars across different countries
posts.excerpt: We ran the numbers on everything — rent, groceries, utilities, healthcare, dining out — and the difference between the US and our top destination countries is staggering.
posts.content:
We've been tracking our monthly expenses for the past two years to build an honest comparison. Our current budget in suburban Ohio runs about forty-eight hundred dollars a month. That includes the mortgage, two car payments, groceries, utilities, health insurance premiums, and the usual household costs. Now compare that to what we'd spend in Portugal: a two-bedroom apartment in a midsize city runs seven to nine hundred euros. Groceries for two people average three hundred fifty euros. Quality private health insurance costs around one hundred fifty euros per person per month. Our projected monthly budget in Portugal lands at roughly twenty-two hundred euros — less than half of what we're spending now.

The savings are even more dramatic in Southeast Asia. In Chiang Mai, Thailand, a modern furnished apartment costs around four hundred fifty dollars. Eating out at local restaurants runs two to three dollars a meal. Monthly expenses for a couple can come in under fifteen hundred dollars, including good private health insurance. The trade-off is distance from family and the need for a solid internet connection if we plan to work remotely or stay connected back home.

Healthcare costs deserve special attention. Our current US health insurance with a mid-tier plan costs us twelve hundred dollars a month in premiums with a six-thousand-dollar deductible. In Portugal, the national health system is available to residents for a nominal fee, and private insurance with comprehensive coverage runs about eighteen hundred dollars per year for both of us. In Thailand, top-tier international coverage that includes evacuation insurance is roughly two thousand dollars annually. These aren't exotic or risky choices — they're established systems that serve millions of expatriates every day.

We're not saying moving abroad is for everyone. But if you're retired or nearing retirement and watching your budget shrink every year, the numbers demand a serious look. We built a detailed spreadsheet with line items for every expense category — we'll share a downloadable version in a future post.
